pages.title: Abraham in Babylon
pages.content:
A very long time ago, about 4,000 years ago, in the kingdom of Babylon in Mesopotamia, there was a boy named Abraham. In his homeland, people worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun, and statues made from wood and stone. Abraham was a wise boy, as Allah made his heart and mind clear of idols. (See Surah Al-Anbiya: 51.)

Abraham discovered Allah when he was at a very young age. From childhood, his heart was full of hatred for idols. He could not understand how an intelligent person could make a statue and then see it as a god which could help or harm him. He saw that these idols did not eat, drink, or talk. They could not even move from one place to another on their own.

In the kingdom of Babylon, people had a large house of worship full of idols with a space in the middle for their biggest gods. Abraham was surprised to see that when people entered the building, they bowed to the statues and started crying and begging. They talked to the gods, asked for help, and made a wish. But the statues could not hear or understand these prayers and wishes!

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
__historical_entity__:abraham-mesopotamia
The country or place where a person comes from.
Able to learn, understand, and think well.
Asking strongly for help or something needed.
Bent the head or body forward to show respect or worship.
To pray to someone or something and show it great love and respect.

hotspots.title: The Kingdom of Babylon
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) grew up in Babylon, where people worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun and statues.

hotspots.title: A House Full of Idols
hotspots.description: In a large house of worship, people bowed to the statues and begged them for help.

exercises.title: Belief and Evidence
exercises.instructions: Match each name with what Chapter 1 says about it.
exercises.question: Who did what in Babylon?

matchingPairs.right: made Abraham’s heart and mind clear of idols
could not understand why intelligent people worshipped things they made

matchingPairs.left: The people in the house of worship
matchingPairs.right: bowed, cried and begged for help
could not hear or understand any prayer or wish

correctAnswer.Allah: made Abraham’s heart and mind clear of idols
correctAnswer.Young Abraham: could not understand why intelligent people worshipped things they made
correctAnswer.The people in the house of worship: bowed, cried and begged for help
correctAnswer.The statues: could not hear or understand any prayer or wish

exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says “Allah made his heart and mind clear of idols”, that Abraham “could not understand how an intelligent person could make a statue and then see it as a god”, that people “bowed to the statues and started crying and begging”, and that “the statues could not hear or understand these prayers and wishes!”

feedback.correct: Well done! You separated what the people did from what the statues could not do, and that contrast is Abraham’s evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Paragraph 1 is about Allah and Abraham’s heart, paragraph 2 about Abraham’s thoughts, and paragraph 3 about the people and the statues. Match each name with its paragraph.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Could” Mean Here?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 1. Then choose the best meaning of “could”.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He could not understand how an intelligent person could make a statue and then see it as a god which could help or harm him.” In “a god which could help or harm him”, what does “could” show?
options: a power that people believed the statue had
a power that the statue really showed in the chapter
something people were allowed to do in the past
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could” changes its meaning with the context. In “a god which could help or harm him”, it describes a power people believed the statue had. The chapter shows the opposite: “They could not even move from one place to another on their own.” In “He could not understand how …”, “could not” shows that Abraham was unable to accept the idea.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Could” here describes a power that people imagined, not a power the statue really had.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the second paragraph: The statues “could not even move … on their own”. So who believed they could help or harm?

languageFocusExercises.title: Short Phrase, Full Clause
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete each sentence with who, which or that. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “named …” or “made from …”?

transformItems.source: … there was a boy named Abraham.
In his homeland, people worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun, and statues made from wood and stone.
transformItems.frame: … and statues [blank] from wood and stone.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A past participle phrase after a noun (“a boy named Abraham”, “statues made from wood and stone”) is a short form of a relative clause: “a boy who was named Abraham”, “statues which were made from wood and stone”. The short form makes description compact, so the chapter can give a lot of detail in one sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You turned the compact phrases into full relative clauses.
feedback.incorrect: Use who for a person and which or that for things, then add was/were before the participle: “who was named …”, “which were made …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Placing Events in Time
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 1 with words from the bank. One word is not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which time words place Abraham’s story in the distant past and in his early life?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: A very long time ago, about 4,000 years [blank], in the kingdom of Babylon in Mesopotamia, there was a boy named Abraham. … Abraham discovered Allah [blank] he was at a very young age. [blank] childhood, his heart was full of hatred for idols.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Ago” comes after a period of time and counts back from now (about 4,000 years ago). “When” links an event to a stage of life (when he was at a very young age). “From childhood” gives the starting point of a past state. “Since childhood” would need the present perfect or past perfect (“had been full of …”), so it does not fit with “was”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Ago, when and from each place the story in time in a different way.
feedback.incorrect: Check the first two paragraphs of Chapter 1. Notice that the sentence with “childhood” uses the past simple “was”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Connected Observation
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone who sees something surprising in a new place.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did the person see, and what could they not understand?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can open with a past-time expression, describe a person or object with added detail, use “could/could not” in context, and include a sentence such as “She could not understand how ...”.

feedback.correct: Keep all four sentences focused on the same situation and make the language relationships clear.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the time: “A long time ago, …” or “When …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Last summer, when I visited a big city for the first time, I went to a market near the station.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Describe a person or thing: “… named …”, “… made from …” or “… full of …”
discussionPrompts.example: It was full of small shops made from old wooden boxes.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Use “could” or “could not”.
discussionPrompts.example: I could hear people speaking many languages, but I could not find a single price on the goods.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add: “He could not understand how …”
discussionPrompts.example: I could not understand how the sellers knew what to charge each customer.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How long ago did Abraham live?

iCan: I can describe what people worshipped in Babylon and what Abraham noticed.
I can add detail to a person or thing with words like “named …” or “made from …”.
I can write four sentences about something surprising in a new place.

pages.title: Abraham and His Father’s Idols
pages.content:
Abraham’s father was an idol maker, named Azer. (See Surah Al-An’am: 74.) When Abraham was a young boy, he often used to watch his father while he was making idols. One day, Abraham asked his father, “Why do you put these toys in the house of worship?” Azer replied, “They are not toys, but our gods. We worship them; we show love and respect to them. We ask favors from them and give them presents.” But Abraham used to play with these idols as toys; he rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them.

One day, his father saw Abraham riding the statue of Mardukh (the Chief God of Babylon), and he got angry with him. He told his son not to play with it again.

Abraham asked, “What is this statue, father? It has big ears, bigger than ours.” His father answered, “It is Mardukh, the god of gods, son! These big ears show his deep knowledge.” This made Abraham laugh; he was only seven years old at that time.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
A person whose job is to carve statues that people worship.
Helpful acts or good things given to someone.
A feeling that someone or something is important and deserves honor.
Hit something with the foot.

hotspots.title: Azer’s Workshop
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) often watched his father, Azer, make idols with his own hands.

hotspots.title: The Statue of Mardukh
hotspots.description: Azer said that Mardukh’s big ears showed deep knowledge, and young Abraham (pbuh) laughed.

exercises.title: A Human-Made God?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports best.
exercises.question: Azer said that Mardukh’s big ears showed his deep knowledge. Why did this make Abraham laugh?
options: His father had told him that the idols were only toys.
He knew that a statue he rode and kicked could not have any knowledge.
He was happy that his father allowed him to play with Mardukh.
exercises.explanation: Abraham watched his father make the idols, and he “rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them.” So he could see that a made statue with big ears could not really know anything. Azer said the opposite: “They are not toys, but our gods,” and he told Abraham not to play with Mardukh again.

feedback.correct: Right! Abraham treated the statues like toys, so the idea of a statue with “deep knowledge” seemed funny to him.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph again. What did Azer say the idols were, and what did Abraham do with them?

languageFocusExercises.title: Again and Again, or One Time?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Again and again, or only one time? Put each part in the right group.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which parts were habits, and which happened only once?

items: he often used to watch his father
Abraham used to play with these idols as toys
he rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them
One day, Abraham asked his father
His father answered, “It is Mardukh, the god of gods, son!”
This made Abraham laugh

Again and again (a habit): he often used to watch his father
Abraham used to play with these idols as toys
he rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them
Only one time (a single event): One day, Abraham asked his father
His father answered, “It is Mardukh, the god of gods, son!”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Used to + verb” describes a habit in an earlier period of life. Once “used to” sets up the habit, the past simple can continue it: “he rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them” describes the same repeated play. “One day” moves the story to one particular event, told in the past simple.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated repeated childhood behavior from single events.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “used to”, “often” and “sometimes” for habits, and “One day” for a single event. “He rode on their backs” follows “used to play”, so it is part of the same habit.

languageFocusExercises.title: Habit, Background, Event
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 2.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form shows a past habit, an action in progress, and a single event?

formChoices.sentence: When Abraham was a young boy, he often [choice] watch his father …
… while he [choice] idols.
One day, his father [choice] Abraham riding the statue of Mardukh (the Chief God of Babylon), and he got angry with him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Used to + base verb = a past habit (“used to watch”). “Was used to” means “was familiar with”, and “use to” is only correct after did/didn’t. While + was/were + -ing = an action in progress in the background (“while he was making idols”). One day + past simple = one finished event (“his father saw Abraham”).

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right form for a habit, a background action and one event.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Was it repeated, was it in progress at that time, or did it happen once? Then check the first two paragraphs of Chapter 2.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong word or phrase, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct a contrast, a comparison and a reported instruction?

errorItems.sentence: Azer replied, “They are not toys, and our gods.”
Abraham asked, “What is this statue, father? It has big ears, more bigger than ours.”
He told his son don’t play with it again.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not … but …” rejects one idea and replaces it with another: “not toys, but our gods”. Short adjectives form the comparative with -er, never with “more … -er”: “bigger than ours”. To report a negative instruction, use tell + person + not to + verb: “He told his son not to play with it again.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the contrast, the comparative and the reported instruction.
feedback.incorrect: Compare each sentence with Chapter 2: Azer’s reply, Abraham’s question about the ears, and the end of the second paragraph.

languageFocusExercises.title: Describe a Past Routine and a Turning Point
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about a childhood habit and one day you remember.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did you use to do, and what happened one day?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can begin with “I used to ...”, add “while ... was/were -ing”, shift with “One day ...”, and finish with a reported instruction such as “My teacher told me not to ...” or a comparison such as “It was bigger than ...”.

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences in one clear time sequence and make the turning point easy to follow.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give a habit: “I used to …”
discussionPrompts.example: When I was eight, I used to walk to school with my older brother every morning.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Add what else was happening: “… while … was/were …ing.”
discussionPrompts.example: While he was talking to his friends, I usually watched the birds in the park.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give one event: “One day, …”
discussionPrompts.example: One day, I saw a small dog shaking under a bench.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add “… told me (not) to …” or compare with “… than …”
discussionPrompts.example: My brother told me not to touch it, so we called our teacher, and she found its owner.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What was Abraham’s father’s job?
beforeYouRead.quote: Abraham’s father was an idol maker, named Azer.

iCan: I can tell how Abraham played with his father’s idols.
I can tell an old habit (“used to …”) from one event (“One day …”).
I can write about a childhood habit and one day I remember.

pages.title: Searching for the True Creator
pages.content:
Years passed, and Abraham grew into a young man. Although he always wondered about Allah, he also knew that Allah could not be a statue. It made him sad to see the people of the kingdom; they were still showing love and respect to idols. On the other hand, Abraham was in search of one true Creator.

One night, Abraham left his home to take a walk in the countryside. On a nearby mountain, he found a cave, sat there, and started thinking about Allah. Then he stood up and looked up at the beautiful sky. He saw a bright star and wondered, “Could this be my Lord?” But when it disappeared, he said, “I will not show respect to it or worship it because it sets and disappears.” He then saw the shining moon and said, “Could this be my Lord?” But when the moon faded, he understood that it could not be his Lord.

vocabulary.definition: The One who brought everything into existence and controls it.
Land outside towns and cities.
A natural hollow place in a mountain or rock.
Gradually became less visible or disappeared.

hotspots.title: The Cave
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) sat in a cave on a nearby mountain and started thinking about Allah.

hotspots.title: The Star and the Moon
hotspots.description: The star disappeared and the moon faded, so Abraham (pbuh) understood that neither could be his Lord.

exercises.title: A Pattern in the Sky
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham decide that the star and the moon could not be his Lord?
options: Neither of them stayed: The star set and the moon faded.
They were smaller and less bright than the sun.
He saw them from a cave, far away from the people.
exercises.explanation: About the star Abraham said, “I will not show respect to it or worship it because it sets and disappears.” Then, “when the moon faded, he understood that it could not be his Lord.” Something that changes and goes away cannot be the Creator.

feedback.correct: Yes! Both of them disappeared, and something that disappears cannot be the Creator.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the chapter again. Look at what happened to the star and to the moon, and at the word “because”.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Still” Tell Us?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 3. Then choose what “still” tells us.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Years passed, and Abraham grew into a young man. … It made him sad to see the people of the kingdom; they were still showing love and respect to idols.” What does “still” tell us about the people?
options: They continued to do this; nothing had changed over the years.
They were quiet and did not move, like the idols in the temple.
They started doing this again after a break of many years.
They did this for the first time when Abraham was a young man.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Still” (before the main verb, after be) shows that a situation continues and has not changed, often when we expect a change. Years passed and Abraham grew up, but the people were still showing love and respect to idols. The continuous form “were showing” adds that this was ongoing. That is why it made Abraham sad.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Still” shows that the people’s behavior continued without change.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the first words of Chapter 3: “Years passed …”. What did not change in all those years?

languageFocusExercises.title: Linking Ideas in Abraham’s Search
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 3 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which linking words show contrast, a change of viewpoint, purpose and reason?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: [blank] he always wondered about Allah, he also knew that Allah could not be a statue. It made him sad to see the people of the kingdom; they were still showing love and respect to idols. [blank], Abraham was in search of one true Creator. One night, Abraham left his home [blank] take a walk in the countryside. … “I will not show respect to it or worship it, [blank] it sets and disappears.”
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Although + clause” holds two ideas together: Abraham still had questions about Allah, but he was sure of one thing. “On the other hand” moves from the people to Abraham’s different position. “To + verb” gives the purpose of an action (left his home to take a walk). “Because” gives the reason for a decision. “Despite” and “because of” cannot be followed by a full clause (subject + verb); they need a noun.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right link for contrast, viewpoint, purpose and reason.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Is it a contrast, a new viewpoint, a purpose (why he left home), or a reason (why he will not worship the star)? Then check Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: Asking and Concluding
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence. Item 1: report the question. Item 2: use Abraham’s words.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does a question or a conclusion change when we report it?

transformItems.source: He saw a bright star and wondered, “Could this be my Lord?”
transformItems.frame: He saw a bright star and wondered [blank] his Lord.

transformItems.source: But when the moon faded, he understood that it could not be his Lord.
transformItems.frame: But when the moon faded, he said, “[blank] Allah.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses if or whether and statement word order: “Could this be my Lord?” → “He wondered if it could be his Lord.” A reported conclusion often moves back in time: Abraham’s thought “It cannot be my Lord” becomes “he understood that it could not be his Lord”. Together these forms build a reasoning chain: test a possibility, then report the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Well done. You moved between direct words and reported thinking.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: start with if or whether and put the subject before the verb. Item 2: use Abraham’s own words, for example “It can’t be …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Short Reasoning Chain
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone thinking about two possible reasons for something.
languageFocusExercises.question: What are the two possible reasons, and what does the person decide?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use “Although ...”, “On the other hand ...”, “Could this be ...?”, “because ...”, and “I understood/realized that ...” in one coherent line of reasoning.

feedback.correct: Keep all four sentences focused on one situation and make the conclusion follow from the evidence.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Show a contrast: “Although …, …” or “On the other hand, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Although my phone was fully charged in the morning, the battery was almost empty at lunchtime.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what the person did next: “Then …” or “… to + verb”
discussionPrompts.example: I opened the settings to check the battery, and then I looked at my apps.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Test an idea: “Could this be …? … because …”
discussionPrompts.example: I wondered, “Could this be the new game?” because I had played it all morning.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the answer: “I understood that …”
discussionPrompts.example: In the end, I realized that the game was using most of the battery.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. Where did Abraham sit and start thinking about Allah?
options: in a cave on a nearby mountain
beforeYouRead.quote: On a nearby mountain, he found a cave, sat there, and started thinking about Allah.

iCan: I can explain how Abraham searched for the true Creator.
I can test an idea with “Could this be …?” and give my conclusion.
I can compare two possible explanations for an everyday event.

pages.title: Abraham Receives Guidance
pages.content:
Abraham stayed until sunrise, and when he saw the bright sun, he wondered, “Could this be my Lord? It is bigger.”

But when it set, he understood that Allah could not be one of the creations. Allah is the Creator of everything. Abraham prostrated himself and asked Allah for help. He said, “If Allah doesn’t show me the right way, I will be on the wrong path.” (See Surah Al-An’am: 77.)

He recognized that he should guide his people because Allah chose him to be His Messenger.

Prophet Abraham (pbuh) went home and told his father, “O my father, follow me: I will guide you on the right way. Stop worshipping idols.” His father grew angry and said, “Do you reject my gods? If you do not stop speaking like this, I will stone you. Leave here now.”

vocabulary.definition: The time when the sun first appears in the morning.
Everything Allah has made, such as the sun, the moon and the stars.
Put the forehead to the ground in worship.
To throw rocks at someone to hurt or kill them.

hotspots.title: The Setting Sun
hotspots.description: Even the big, bright sun set, so Abraham (pbuh) understood that Allah is the Creator of everything.

hotspots.title: The Right Way
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) prostrated himself, asked Allah to guide him, and then called his father to the right way.

exercises.title: From the Sun to His Father
exercises.instructions: Put the events of Chapter 4 in the right order.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham saw the bright sun and wondered if it could be his Lord.
When the sun set, Abraham understood that Allah could not be one of the creations.
Abraham prostrated himself and asked Allah for help.
Abraham asked his father to follow him and stop worshipping idols.
Azer grew angry and told him to leave.

exercises.explanation: Abraham first wondered about the sun (“It is bigger”). When it set, he understood that “Allah is the Creator of everything.” He prostrated himself and asked for help, then went home and said, “O my father, follow me.” His father grew angry and said, “Leave here now.”

feedback.correct: Great! You followed Abraham from watching the sky, to his prayer, to his call to his father.
feedback.incorrect: Follow the chapter step by step: The sky comes before the prayer, and the prayer comes before Abraham goes home.

languageFocusExercises.title: Same Form, Different Purpose
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the two “if” sentences from Chapter 4. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: (1) Abraham: “If Allah doesn’t show me the right way, I will be on the wrong path.” (2) His father: “If you do not stop speaking like this, I will stone you.” Both sentences use If + present, will + verb. How are they different?
options: In (1), Abraham shows that he needs Allah’s guidance; in (2), his father makes a threat.
Sentence (1) is about the past; sentence (2) is about the future, so they use different times.
In (1), Abraham makes a threat; in (2), his father asks for help.
Both sentences are promises: Each speaker says he will help the other person.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: If + present simple, will + verb talks about a possible future situation and its result. The form is the same in both sentences, but the purpose depends on the speaker. Abraham is praying and asking for help, so his sentence shows his need for guidance. His father is angry, so his sentence is a threat: Stop, or this will happen.

feedback.correct: Correct. The same grammar can express a need or a threat, depending on who speaks and why.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what each speaker is doing: Abraham has just asked Allah for help, and his father “grew angry”. Both sentences are about the future.

languageFocusExercises.title: Time and Role
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 4.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which forms mark an end point in time and the role someone is chosen for?

formChoices.sentence: Abraham stayed [choice] sunrise, and when he saw the bright sun, he wondered, “Could this be my Lord? It is bigger.”
He recognized that he … because Allah chose him [choice] His Messenger.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Until” marks the end point of an action that continues (he stayed … until sunrise). Choose + person + to be + role says what someone is chosen for: Allah chose him to be His Messenger.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used until for an end point, the present simple after if, and chose + person + to be.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: no “will” after “if” here, and chose him + to + verb. Check the first three paragraphs of Chapter 4.

languageFocusExercises.title: Duty and Direct Instructions
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong words, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct the verb forms after “should” and “stop”?

errorItems.sentence: He recognized that he should to guide his people …
… told his father, “O my father, follow me: I will guide you on the right way. Stop worship idols.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Should + base verb” (no “to”) expresses a duty; here “because …” gives the reason for that duty. Direct instructions use the imperative: “Follow me”, “Leave here now”. After “stop”, use -ing to mean “do not do this any more”: “Stop worshipping idols”. “Stop to worship” would mean stopping in order to worship, which is the opposite meaning.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the modal verb and the imperative.
feedback.incorrect: Check the third and fourth paragraphs of Chapter 4: “he should … his people” and Abraham’s words to his father.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Responsibility-and-Response Scene
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone who sees a duty and tells others.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the duty, and how do other people answer?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can combine “when ...”, “should ... because ...”, a direct imperative, and “If ... , I will ...” while keeping one clear situation.

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences connected and make the conditional response logically follow from the situation.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Start with “When …” or “Until …”
discussionPrompts.example: When I saw our messy classroom after the party, I realized that someone had to clean it.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give a duty and a reason: “We should … because …”
discussionPrompts.example: As class monitor this week, I should organize the cleaning because everyone uses this room.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give one clear instruction: “Follow …”, “Stop …” or “Leave …”
discussionPrompts.example: “Pick up your cups and put them in the recycling bin, please,” I said to my classmates.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give an answer: “If …, I will …”
discussionPrompts.example: One friend smiled and said, “If you carry the chairs, I will clean the board.”

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: Why did Abraham (pbuh) first think the sun could be his Lord?

iCan: I can explain what Abraham (pbuh) understood when the sun set.
I can say what someone should do and why.
I can write a short school scene with a duty, an instruction and an if-sentence.

pages.title: Abraham Calls His People
pages.content: Abraham (pbuh) was very sad for his father. Then, he went to the people of the kingdom and tried to show them the right way: “O people! I have turned my face towards Allah. I do not worship your idols because Allah is the one and only true God!” People got furious when they heard him. Abraham (pbuh) said to them, “Why do you worship these statues? They have no power to help or harm you.” People replied, “We saw our fathers worship them; because of this, we do the same.” Abraham (pbuh) did not give up and told them, “My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them, and heals me when I am sick. Your statues have no power to do these.” He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs. They ignored him, though.

vocabulary.definition: To stop trying to do something.
To hurt or damage someone or something.
Makes a sick or injured person well again.
To think again about an idea or belief.

hotspots.title: Public Call
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) openly told his people that he did not worship their idols because Allah is the one true God.

hotspots.title: Following Their Fathers
hotspots.description: The people had only one reason for worshipping the statues: their fathers had worshipped them too.

exercises.title: Tradition or Evidence?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports best.
exercises.question: The people said, “We saw our fathers worship them.” Why was this a weak reason?
options: The statues gave them food and drink when they needed it.
Their fathers had seen the statues heal sick people in the temple many years ago.
It was only a habit, and the statues had no power to help or harm them.
exercises.explanation: The people gave only one reason: “We saw our fathers worship them; because of this, we do the same.” Abraham showed the problem: The statues “have no power to help or harm you,” while Allah gives him food and drink and heals him when he is sick.

feedback.correct: Right! Doing something because our fathers did it is not proof. Abraham asked his people to think about the evidence.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the people’s answer with Abraham’s words in the middle of the paragraph. Who gives food, drink and healing, and what can the statues do?

languageFocusExercises.title: Words for Effort and Response
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each word or phrase from Chapter 5 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these words tell us about Abraham’s effort and the people’s response?

matchingPairs.right: became very angry
kept trying
think again about
paid no attention to

matchingPairs.left: though (at the end of a sentence)
matchingPairs.right: however

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Give up” is a phrasal verb meaning “stop trying”, so “did not give up” means he kept trying. “Reconsider” = re- (again) + consider (think about). “Ignore” means to pay no attention on purpose. At the end of a sentence, “though” works like “however”: “They ignored him, though.” shows a result that is different from what Abraham hoped for.

feedback.correct: Correct. These words show Abraham’s continued effort and the people’s refusal.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 5 again: “Abraham (pbuh) did not give up … He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs. They ignored him, though.”

languageFocusExercises.title: Reasons and Situations
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word or phrase to complete each sentence from Chapter 5.
languageFocusExercises.question: When do we use because, because of, and when?

formChoices.sentence: “I do not worship your idols [choice] Allah is the one and only true God!”
People replied, “We saw our fathers worship them; [choice], we do the same.”
“My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them, and heals me [choice] I am sick.”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because” is followed by a clause with a subject and verb (because Allah is …). “Because of” is followed by a noun or pronoun (because of this). “When + clause” tells us the situation in which something happens (when I am sick). “During” is followed by a noun, not a clause.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each linker with the kind of words that follow it.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what comes after each gap: a full clause (subject + verb) or nothing but a comma? Then check Abraham’s and the people’s words in Chapter 5.

languageFocusExercises.title: Wanting Someone to Act
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence from Chapter 5 so that it keeps the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can we say what we want someone to do?

transformItems.source: He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs.
transformItems.frame: Abraham said to the people, “I want [blank] your beliefs.”

transformItems.source: People got furious when they heard him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: To say what we want another person to do, use want + person + to + verb: “I want you to reconsider …” (not “I want that you reconsider”). A when-clause can come after or before the main clause. When it comes first, put a comma after it: “When people heard him, they got furious.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You used want + person + to and moved the when-clause correctly.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: Abraham speaks to the people, so “them” becomes “you”. Item 2: the when-clause now comes first, so it needs its own subject.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Persuasion Scene
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone trying to change another person’s mind.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the person try, and what is the answer?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use because, try to, not give up or continue, want someone to..., and though/but to keep one coherent situation.

feedback.correct: Keep all four sentences in one situation and make the contrast logically follow from the attempt.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give a belief and a reason with “because”.
discussionPrompts.example: I decided to cycle to school because it is healthy and cheap.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Show an attempt: “… tried to …”
discussionPrompts.example: I tried to persuade my best friend to cycle with me.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Show they kept trying: “… did not give up” or “… wanted … to …”
discussionPrompts.example: I did not give up, and I wanted him to try it for just one week.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give a different answer with “but” or “though”.
discussionPrompts.example: He agreed to think about it, though he still takes the bus every day.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How did Abraham (pbuh) feel about his father?
beforeYouRead.quote: Abraham (pbuh) was very sad for his father.

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) called his people and how they answered.
I can give a reason with “because” or “because of”.
I can describe a polite attempt to change a friend’s mind.

roles.name: Chapter 2 Expert
