steps: Read your chapter again. Note two key facts and copy one sentence from the book that supports each fact.
Teach your facts to the group in your own words, then read your two sentences aloud.
Listen to the others and build one shared timeline from Abraham as a young boy to his call to the people of the kingdom.

Together, complete this sentence with three reasons, each backed by a quote: “Abraham knew that the idols could not be gods because …”. For example, the book says: “They could not even move from one place to another on their own.”
groupTask.share: Each group presents its timeline and its three reasons, and reads one quote aloud for each reason.
groupTask.solo: Make a timeline of Chapters 1–5 with one event from each chapter, and write one reason why the idols could not be gods, with a quote from the book.

pages.title: Abraham Enters the Temple
pages.content:
Prophet Abraham (pbuh) decided to show them the foolishness of their beliefs. He made a plan to destroy all their idols, but he did not tell anyone what he was going to do. There was a big celebration soon. All the people usually went outside of town, so he got an axe and waited until the whole town was empty. He went into the big temple and saw all the statues standing there. There were plates of food in front of them, and Abraham (pbuh) jokingly asked them, “Why don’t you eat the food? It is getting cold.” Offering food to these statues was so ridiculous.

Abraham (pbuh) began to break the idols, one after another, until they were all broken. He did not break the largest statue in the temple. He hung the axe around its neck and then hurried back home.

vocabulary.definition: Lack of good sense or wise thinking.
A special event when people gather for a happy occasion.
A tool with a sharp metal head used for cutting.
Very silly or unreasonable.

hotspots.title: Empty Town
hotspots.description: Everyone went outside the town for a big celebration, so Abraham (pbuh) entered the temple alone.

hotspots.title: Food for the Idols
hotspots.description: The statues could not eat the food in front of them, which showed how helpless they were.

exercises.title: The Temple Plan
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 6.
exercises.question: Abraham broke every statue in the temple, even the largest one.
exercises.explanation: Abraham broke the idols “one after another,” but “He did not break the largest statue in the temple. He hung the axe around its neck and then hurried back home.” This was part of his plan.

feedback.correct: Correct! He did not break the largest statue. He hung the axe around its neck.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 6 again. What did Abraham do with the largest statue?

languageFocusExercises.title: A Plan Seen from the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 6. Then choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “He made a plan to destroy all their idols, but he did not tell anyone what he was going to do.” What does “what he was going to do” mean here?
options: the action he had planned for later; at that moment it had not happened yet
the action he was doing at that exact moment, while he was talking to people
an action he did many times before, as a habit, in the temple
an action he had already finished before he made the plan
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was/were going to + verb” is the future seen from a moment in the past. When Abraham made his plan, breaking the idols was still in the future, so the chapter says “what he was going to do”. Together with “decided to” and “made a plan to”, it shows that his action was deliberate, not an accident.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Was going to” shows a planned action that was still in the future at that time.
feedback.incorrect: Think about the order of events in Chapter 6: first he made the plan, then he waited, and only later did he break the idols.

languageFocusExercises.title: Habit, Result and Timing
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 6 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words show a habit, a result and a time limit?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: There was a big celebration soon. All the people [blank] went outside of town, [blank] he got an axe and waited [blank] the whole town was empty.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Usually” describes what normally happened at celebrations (a habit). “So” introduces the result: The town would be empty, so Abraham got an axe. “Until” marks the point he had to wait for before he could act. “Because” would give a reason, not a result, and “by” cannot be followed by a clause here.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the habit, the result and the time limit.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: What normally happened, what did Abraham do as a result, and how long did he wait? Then check the first paragraph of Chapter 6.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build the Final Sentence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to rebuild this sentence from Chapter 6.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abraham do after he broke the idols?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: The chapter uses “began to break the idols, one after another, until they were all broken” to show the start, the repetition and the end of the action. Then a short negative sentence shows what Abraham chose not to do: “He did not break the largest statue in the temple.” The last sentence puts two actions in order with “and then”: First he hung the axe around its neck, and then he hurried back home.

feedback.correct: Well done. You put the last two actions in order with “and then”.
feedback.incorrect: Start with “He hung”, say what he hung and where, then add the second action with “and then”. Check the last paragraph of Chapter 6.

languageFocusExercises.title: Describe a Deliberate Plan
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone carrying out a careful plan.
languageFocusExercises.question: What is the plan, and how does it end?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can combine decided/planned to, usually or a background situation, so, until, began to, did not + verb and and then.

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences in one coherent situation and make each action logically lead to the next.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the plan: “… decided to …” or “… planned to …”
discussionPrompts.example: My sister decided to surprise our mother with a homemade cake.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Describe the chance, and join with “so”.
discussionPrompts.example: Our mother usually visits our grandmother on Saturday mornings, so my sister bought everything she needed on Friday.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Use “until” to show when the action began or ended.
discussionPrompts.example: She waited until our mother left the house, and then she began to bake.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Show the end: “… did not …” and “… and then …”
discussionPrompts.example: She did not tell anyone about it. She hid the cake in the fridge and then cleaned the kitchen.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What was in front of the statues?
beforeYouRead.quote: There were plates of food in front of them

iCan: I can tell how Abraham (pbuh) carried out his plan in the temple.
I can talk about a plan with “was going to” and “until”.
I can describe a careful plan from start to finish.

pages.title: The Broken Idols
pages.content:
The next day, when people went to the temple to pray to their idols, they were shocked to see all the statues were broken into many pieces. They all gathered around the smashed idols. They wondered and tried to find out who did this. “We heard a young man speaking against our gods,” they remembered. “His name was Abraham.” They found Abraham (pbuh) and brought him into the temple. They asked him, “Did you harm our gods in this way?” Abraham (pbuh) calmly replied, “It was this statue there, the biggest of them all; ask that statue if it can speak!”

The people were displeased with what they heard and said, “You are well aware that these idols don’t speak!” Abraham (pbuh) replied, “Then why do you worship things that can’t speak or see or even protect themselves? Have you gone mad?”

They looked at each other in shame because their thoughts and feelings told them that Abraham (pbuh) was right. But they were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth and admit they were wrong. If they accepted that Abraham (pbuh) was right, then it meant their forefathers were wrong, as well. They started shouting, “Burn him! Burn him! In the name of our gods, punish him!” (See Surah Al-Anbiya: 68; Surah Al-Ankabut: 24.)

vocabulary.definition: Broken violently into many pieces.
Unhappy or annoyed about something.
A painful feeling caused by knowing something is wrong.
Too proud to accept the truth or a mistake.

hotspots.title: Smashed Statues
hotspots.description: The people found their idols smashed and saw that they had not been able to protect themselves.

hotspots.title: Public Questioning
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) used the people’s own words to show that their idols could not speak or protect themselves.

exercises.title: Shame and Pride
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports best.
exercises.question: The people felt that Abraham was right. Why did they still shout, “Burn him!”?
options: They were too proud to admit that they and their forefathers were wrong.
They believed that the largest statue had really broken the others.
King Nimrod had ordered them to punish Abraham.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 says, “They looked at each other in shame because their thoughts and feelings told them that Abraham (pbuh) was right. But they were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth.” Accepting it “meant their forefathers were wrong, as well.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Their pride was stronger than the truth they felt. Admitting a mistake needs honesty and courage.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 7 again. Look for the word “But” after they felt shame.

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Kinds of Questions
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is it a question in the speaker’s words, or inside a longer sentence? Sort the parts.
languageFocusExercises.question: How is the word order different when a question sits inside a longer sentence?

items: They asked him, “Did you harm our gods in this way?”
“Then why do you worship things that can’t speak …?”
“Have you gone mad?”

dragDropGroups.group: A question idea inside a longer sentence
items: They wondered and tried to find out who did this.
ask that statue if it can speak!

The speaker’s exact question: They asked him, “Did you harm our gods in this way?”
“Then why do you worship things that can’t speak …?”
A question idea inside a longer sentence: They wondered and tried to find out who did this.
ask that statue if it can speak!

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A direct question uses question word order (Did you harm …? Have you gone …? Why do you …?) and a question mark. Inside a longer sentence, after words like find out or ask … if, the question idea has no question mark and uses statement word order: ask that statue if it can speak (not “if can it speak”). In “find out who did this”, who is the subject and did is the main verb, so the order is the same as a statement.

feedback.correct: Correct. You noticed that question ideas inside a sentence keep statement word order.
feedback.incorrect: Look for quotation marks, a question mark and an auxiliary before the subject (did you, have you, do you). Those are direct questions.

languageFocusExercises.title: Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong words, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct the verb forms after heard and shocked, and the word order after what?

errorItems.sentence: “We heard a young man to speak against our gods,” they remembered.
The people were displeased with what did they hear and said, “You are well aware that these idols don’t speak!”
… they were shocked to seeing all the statues were broken into many pieces.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: After hear + person, use -ing (or the base verb), never to + verb: “We heard a young man speaking against our gods.” The -ing form shows the action was in progress. After what inside a longer sentence, use statement word order and no did: “what they heard”. After adjectives of feeling such as shocked, use to + base verb to say what caused the feeling: “shocked to see”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the verb patterns and the word order after “what”.
feedback.incorrect: Use -ing after “heard a young man”, statement word order after “what”, and to + base verb after “shocked”. Compare with Chapter 7.

languageFocusExercises.title: Reason, Result and Consequence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word to complete each sentence from Chapter 7.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why were the people ashamed but still did not accept the truth?

formChoices.sentence: They looked at each other in shame [choice] their thoughts and feelings told them that Abraham (pbuh) was right.
But they were so arrogant [choice] they couldn’t accept the truth and admit they were wrong.
If they accepted that Abraham (pbuh) was right, then it [choice] their forefathers were wrong, as well.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because” gives the reason for their shame. “So + adjective + that” shows a very strong quality and its result: They were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth. “If … then …” shows the consequence they were afraid of; the story is in the past, so the result verb is also past (meant).

feedback.correct: Correct. You linked the reason, the strong result and the consequence.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 7. Ask which word gives a reason, which word completes “so arrogant …”, and which tense fits a story told in the past.

languageFocusExercises.title: Report a Disagreement Clearly
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about a disagreement. Do not retell Chapter 7.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did people hear, and how did they react?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can combine heard/saw/remembered, find out who/what/why, because or but, and an if...then consequence.

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences connected so the information, reaction, and consequence form one coherent situation.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what someone heard, saw or remembered.
discussionPrompts.example: Yesterday, I heard two classmates arguing about a football match.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Add a question idea: “… wanted to find out who / what / why …”
discussionPrompts.example: Our teacher tried to find out why they were so upset.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Explain a reaction with “because”, “but” or “so … that”.
discussionPrompts.example: One of them was angry because he thought the referee was unfair.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add “If …, …” or a clear result.
discussionPrompts.example: They watched the video together, and in the end they agreed that the goal was fair.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. Who did Abraham (pbuh) tell the people to ask?
beforeYouRead.quote: It was this statue there, the biggest of them all; ask that statue if it can speak!

iCan: I can explain why the people felt ashamed but did not accept the truth.
I can put a question inside a longer sentence, like “find out who did this”.
I can report a disagreement clearly and calmly.

pages.title: Preparing the Great Fire
pages.content:
Firewood was collected for the fire for days.

The fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it. However, Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm because he trusted Allah. He knew that Allah would never leave him alone, and that whatever happened, it would be for his own good.

News about the fire traveled very fast and far. People from many different towns came to see what would happen. The fire was finally ready. The heat was so strong that even birds couldn’t fly over the rising flames.

Prophet Abraham’s (pbuh) hands and feet were tied, and he was placed on a catapult. A catapult was a kind of machine which was used to throw Abraham (pbuh) into the fire.

Abraham (pbuh) was thrown straight into huge flames. At that moment, Angel Gabriel came to him and asked, “Is there anything you wish for?” Abraham (pbuh) only said, “Nothing from you!”

Allah commanded the fire to be cool for Prophet Abraham (pbuh), and it turned out to be safe for him. (See Surah Al-Anbiya: 69.) It only burnt the ropes on his hands and feet. He sat in the middle of the fire safely. The fire turned into a garden. Prophet Abraham (pbuh) emerged in good condition when the flames cooled.

vocabulary.definition: Wood that is cut and used to make a fire.
To come near something or someone.
The bright, burning parts of a fire.
An old machine used to throw heavy objects.

hotspots.title: A Huge Fire
hotspots.description: The fire was so big that no one could approach it, but Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm and trusted Allah.

hotspots.title: Cool and Safe
hotspots.description: Allah commanded the fire to be cool and safe for Abraham (pbuh), and he came out unharmed.

exercises.title: Calm Before the Fire
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: The fire was so big that people could not come near it. Why did Abraham stay calm?
options: Angel Gabriel had already told him that the fire would not burn him at all.
He trusted Allah and knew that whatever happened would be for his own good.
Many people from other towns had come to help him and to put out the fire.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8 says, “Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm because he trusted Allah. He knew that Allah would never leave him alone, and that whatever happened, it would be for his own good.” Gabriel came only later, and the people from other towns came “to see what would happen.”

feedback.correct: Right! His calm came from his trust in Allah, not from knowing how the story would end.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 8 again. Find the sentence with “because”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Who Did the Action?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Does each sentence say who did the action? Sort the parts of Chapter 8.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why does the chapter sometimes not say who did an action?

dragDropGroups.group: We are not told who did the action
items: Firewood was collected for the fire for days.
Prophet Abraham’s (pbuh) hands and feet were tied
Abraham (pbuh) was thrown straight into huge flames.
Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm
Angel Gabriel came to him
It only burnt the ropes on his hands and feet.

We are not told who did the action: Firewood was collected for the fire for days.
Prophet Abraham’s (pbuh) hands and feet were tied
Abraham (pbuh) was thrown straight into huge flames.
The subject does the action: It only burnt the ropes on his hands and feet.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The passive (was/were + past participle: was collected, were tied, was thrown) puts the focus on what happened to Abraham or the firewood. The people who did these actions are not important here, so the chapter does not name them. In active sentences, the subject does the action: “It only burnt the ropes” – the fire did the burning.

feedback.correct: Correct. You noticed that the passive focuses on what happened, not on who did it.
feedback.incorrect: Look for was/were + past participle. Then ask: Can I find the person who did the action in the sentence?

languageFocusExercises.title: Danger and Calm
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 8 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words show how extreme the fire was and how Abraham reacted?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: The fire was [blank] big [blank] people couldn’t approach it. [blank], Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm [blank] he trusted Allah.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “So + adjective + that” shows a very strong degree and its result: The fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it. (“Such” needs a noun: such a big fire that …). “However,” at the start of a sentence shows a contrast with the sentence before. “Because” gives the reason for Abraham’s calm. “Although” must join two clauses in one sentence, so it cannot stand alone with a comma.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed the degree, the result, the contrast and the reason.
feedback.incorrect: Check the second paragraph of Chapter 8. Which word goes with an adjective (big), and which contrast word can start a sentence followed by a comma?

languageFocusExercises.title: Looking Forward from the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 8.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the chapter talk about the future when the story is told in the past?

formChoices.sentence: He knew that Allah would never leave him alone, and that whatever [choice], it would be for his own good.
People from many different towns came to see what [choice] happen.
A catapult was a kind of machine which was used [choice] throw Abraham (pbuh) into the fire.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: When a story is told in the past, “would” shows the future from that past moment: people came to see what would happen. In the same way, Abraham knew that “whatever happened, it would be for his own good” – both verbs move back from “whatever happens, it will be”. “Was used to + base verb” describes the purpose of an object (it was used to throw). It is different from “used to” for past habits.

feedback.correct: Correct. You kept the future-in-the-past forms and the purpose pattern.
feedback.incorrect: The story is in the past, so the future is expressed with would and a past verb. Read the second, third and fourth paragraphs of Chapter 8 again.

languageFocusExercises.title: Describe Pressure and an Unexpected Outcome
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about a hard situation with a surprising end.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was hard, and what was the surprise at the end?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use so...that, however/because, knew/thought that ... would, and turned out to be/became.

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences connected as one short narrative.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Describe a hard moment: “It was so … that …”
discussionPrompts.example: The exam room was so quiet that I could hear my own heartbeat.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Add a different reaction with “however” or “because”.
discussionPrompts.example: However, I tried to stay calm because I had studied every day for a month.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say what someone expected: “He knew / thought that … would …”
discussionPrompts.example: I thought that the last question would be very difficult.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the surprise: “… turned out to be …”, “… became …” or “… turned into …”
discussionPrompts.example: In fact, it turned out to be the easiest question on the paper.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. What did the fire turn into?
beforeYouRead.quote: The fire turned into a garden.

iCan: I can explain why Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm and what happened to the fire.
I can say what happened to someone without naming who did it.
I can describe a difficult situation with an unexpected result.

pages.title: The Miracle and Nimrod
pages.content:
People were shocked to see that Abraham (pbuh) was not harmed at all. People felt embarrassed by the miracle, yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.

Prophet Abraham (pbuh) tried every way to show them their error; however, their rage didn’t calm down.

Nimrod was the king of Babylon. He also heard about the miracle. He realized that Abraham was not an ordinary person, so he decided to meet him. He called Abraham (pbuh) and asked him, “Who is your God?”

He (pbuh) said, “He is Allah, the One. He gives life and brings death.”

“I can give life and death,” said Nimrod. He ordered his guards to bring two slaves and to put them to death. The guards killed one of the slaves, then Nimrod said, “I let the second slave live; let him go.” The slave was free.

“See! I can also give life and death!” he said to Abraham (pbuh). In response, Prophet Abraham (pbuh) said, “Allah makes the sun rise in the east. Can you make the sun rise from the west?” Naturally, Nimrod was unable to do this; only Allah has the power to do that. This made Nimrod even more angry.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
__historical_entity__:abraham-nimrod
An amazing event that shows Allah’s power and that no human can do.
Very strong anger.
People whose job is to protect a person or place.
Normal and not unusual or special.

hotspots.title: Nimrod’s Claim
hotspots.description: Nimrod claimed that he could give life and death because he let one of the slaves live.

hotspots.title: The Sun from the West
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) asked Nimrod to make the sun rise from the west, and Nimrod could not do it.

exercises.title: Claim and Challenge
exercises.instructions: Match each step of the debate with what was said or done.
exercises.question: How did the debate between Abraham and Nimrod go?

matchingPairs.right: “He is Allah, the One. He gives life and brings death.”
“I can give life and death.”
One slave was killed, and the other was let go.
“Can you make the sun rise from the west?”

correctAnswer.Abraham’s first answer: “He is Allah, the One. He gives life and brings death.”
correctAnswer.Nimrod’s example: One slave was killed, and the other was let go.
correctAnswer.Abraham’s challenge: “Can you make the sun rise from the west?”

exercises.explanation: Nimrod tried to copy Abraham’s words about life and death by deciding what happened to two slaves. Abraham then asked for something only Allah can do: “Can you make the sun rise from the west?” Nimrod “was unable to do this.”

feedback.correct: Well done! You followed the debate from Abraham’s answer to the challenge Nimrod could not meet.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second half of Chapter 9 again. Check who says “I can …” and who asks about the sun.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does “Yet” Show?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 9. Then choose what “yet” shows.
languageFocusExercises.question: “People felt embarrassed by the miracle, yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.” What does “yet” show here?
options: The second idea is surprising after the first: They were embarrassed, but they did not change.
The second idea is the result of the first: They were embarrassed, so they changed.
The second idea has not happened until now.
The second idea happened before the first: They were angry before the miracle.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Between two clauses, “yet” means “but” and shows an unexpected contrast: After such a miracle, we expect people to change, but their anger stayed the same. “However” does the same job in the next sentence: “Prophet Abraham (pbuh) tried every way …; however, their rage didn’t calm down.” This is different from “not … yet” (= not until now).

feedback.correct: Correct. “Yet” joins two ideas that do not fit together as we expect.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: After a miracle, what would we expect people to do? Does the second part of the sentence follow that expectation or go against it?

languageFocusExercises.title: Order, Let and Make
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong word or words, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which verb form follows order, let and make + person or thing?

errorItems.sentence: He ordered his guards bring two slaves and to put them to death.
… then Nimrod said, “I let the second slave to live; let him go.”
“Allah makes the sun rise in the east. Can you make the sun to rise from the west?”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Order and tell use person + to + verb: “ordered his guards to bring”. Let and make use person/thing + base verb with no “to”: “let the second slave live”, “make the sun rise”. Nimrod uses “let” to show his power to allow; Abraham uses “make” to test that claim.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used “to” after order, and the base verb after let and make.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: order + person + to + verb, but let/make + person + verb without “to”. Check Nimrod’s and Abraham’s words in Chapter 9.

languageFocusExercises.title: Inability and Exclusive Power
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write the missing words. Keep the same meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can we say “was unable to” and “only …”?

transformItems.source: Naturally, Nimrod was unable to do this; only Allah has the power to do that.
… only Allah has the power to do that.
transformItems.frame: Allah is the only one [blank] the power to do that.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was unable to + verb” = “could not” or “was not able to”: it states inability in the past, after Nimrod’s claim “I can give life and death”. “Only Allah has …” limits the power to one source; “Allah is the only one who has …” says the same thing with a relative clause.

feedback.correct: Well done. You expressed the same inability and the same limit in a new way.
feedback.incorrect: Item 1: use could not or was not able to + do. Item 2: after “the only one”, add who/that + has.

languageFocusExercises.title: Challenge a Claim with Evidence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say four sentences about someone who says they can do something, and a test.
languageFocusExercises.question: What does the person say, and what does the test show?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use can/can’t, so, however/yet, order/tell/let if natural, and a final result expression such as was unable to or this made....

feedback.correct: Keep the four sentences connected as one short exchange or narrative.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what someone can do, using “can”.
discussionPrompts.example: My little brother said, “I can run to the corner shop and back in one minute.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say why another person tests it, with “so” or “because”.
discussionPrompts.example: I did not believe him, so I decided to test his claim with my watch.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Write the test as a question or an instruction.
discussionPrompts.example: “Run to the shop and back, and I will time you!” I said.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the result: “… was able / unable to …” or “However, …”
discussionPrompts.example: He ran very fast, yet he was unable to do it in less than three minutes.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How did the people feel after the miracle?
beforeYouRead.quote: People felt embarrassed by the miracle, yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.

iCan: I can explain how Abraham (pbuh) answered Nimrod’s claim.
I can show a surprising contrast with “yet” or “however”.
I can test an everyday claim with evidence.

pages.title: Leaving Babylon
pages.content:
Only one woman and one man of his people shared his faith in Allah. The woman’s name was Sarah, and the man’s name was Lot. Lot later became a prophet.

Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message. Therefore, he decided to leave Babylon and travel to other lands to spread Allah’s message. He traveled from Babylon to Syria and Palestine on camelback. It was a long, hot, and tiring journey. During his journey, Abraham (pbuh) married Hagar and asked for a child from Allah so that his child could teach people about Allah. Hagar soon gave birth to Abraham’s (pbuh) first son, named Ishmael.

One day, Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to travel with his wife and little child Ishmael. They all traveled for a long time. Finally, they reached a lonely valley near two small hills, Safa and Marwa. Prophet Abraham (pbuh) told his wife to stay near one of the hills with Ishmael.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-babylon
__historical_entity__:abraham-syria-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-palestine-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-safa-and-marwa-ancient
Strong belief and trust in Allah.
To make an idea or message reach more people.
Riding on the back of the large desert animal with a hump.
Making someone feel that they need rest.

hotspots.title: Toward New Lands
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) left Babylon and traveled to other lands to spread Allah’s message.

hotspots.title: Lonely Valley
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh), Hagar and Ishmael (pbuh) reached a lonely valley near the hills of Safa and Marwa.

exercises.title: Why Leave Babylon?
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham decide to leave Babylon?
options: His father had told him to leave home and never come back to Babylon.
Nobody was going to listen to him, so he went to spread Allah’s message in other lands.
Nimrod ordered him to go to Syria and Palestine and never come back to his kingdom.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says, “Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message. Therefore, he decided to leave Babylon and travel to other lands to spread Allah’s message.” Leaving did not end his mission; it continued it.

feedback.correct: Yes! He did not give up. He took the message to new places.
feedback.incorrect: Read the beginning of the second paragraph again. Find the word “Therefore”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Why? or What Was He Told?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Does each part say why someone acts, or what someone is told to do? Sort them.
languageFocusExercises.question: Does “to + verb” always show purpose?

items: … travel to other lands to spread Allah’s message
… so that his child could teach people about Allah

dragDropGroups.group: Instruction: what someone is told to do
items: Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to travel with his wife …
… told his wife to stay near one of the hills

Purpose: Why someone acts: … travel to other lands to spread Allah’s message
… so that his child could teach people about Allah
Instruction: what someone is told to do: Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to travel with his wife …
… told his wife to stay near one of the hills

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “To + verb” has two different jobs here. After an action, it can give the purpose (travel … to spread Allah’s message = in order to spread it). After command/tell + person, it gives the instruction (commanded Abraham to travel, told his wife to stay). “So that + could” also gives a purpose, with its own subject: So that his child could teach people.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated purpose from instruction, even though both use “to”.
feedback.incorrect: Look before “to”: is there a verb like command or tell + a person? Then it is an instruction. Can you add “in order” before “to”? Then it is a purpose.

languageFocusExercises.title: Decision and Journey
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word or form to complete each sentence from Chapter 10.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which forms show a decision and the stages of a long journey?

formChoices.sentence: Therefore, he decided [choice] Babylon and travel to other lands to spread Allah’s message.
[choice] his journey, Abraham (pbuh) married Hagar …
They all traveled for a long time. [choice], they reached a lonely valley near two small hills, Safa and Marwa.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Decide” is followed by to + verb (decided to leave … and travel). “During + noun” places an event inside a longer period (during his journey); “while” needs a clause (while he was traveling). “Finally” marks the end point after a long process; “at first” and “firstly” introduce a beginning.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the forms for a decision, a time period and an end point.
feedback.incorrect: Check what follows each gap: A verb, a noun (his journey), or a comma after a long time of travel. Then read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 10.

languageFocusExercises.title: From Thought to Report
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Change the reported sentence into Abraham’s own thought.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does “was going to” change when we use the speaker’s own words?

transformItems.source: Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Realized that … was going to” reports a future prediction from a past moment. In Abraham’s own words, the prediction is in the present: “Nobody is going to listen to my message.” This realization leads to a result: “Therefore, he decided to leave Babylon.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You changed the reported prediction back into direct thought.
feedback.incorrect: In direct words, “was going to” becomes “is going to”, and “his message” becomes “my message”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain a Purposeful Journey
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five sentences about a journey or a move to a new place.
languageFocusExercises.question: Why does the person go, and where does the journey end?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use realized that, therefore/so, decided to, to + verb or so that, during, soon, one day, and finally.

feedback.correct: Keep the sentences connected as one short narrative, not five unrelated statements.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what the person realizes.
discussionPrompts.example: Last year, my family realized that our flat was too small for five people.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give the decision, with “so” or “therefore”.
discussionPrompts.example: Therefore, we decided to move to a bigger house in another town.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give the reason: “… to …” or “… so that …”
discussionPrompts.example: We chose a house near a park so that my little sisters could play outside.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add one event on the way.
discussionPrompts.example: During the move, our old car broke down on the motorway, and we waited two hours for help.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Give the end: “Finally, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Finally, we arrived late at night, tired but happy.

beforeYouRead.question: Look at the picture. How did Abraham (pbuh) travel from Babylon to Syria and Palestine?
beforeYouRead.quote: He traveled from Babylon to Syria and Palestine on camelback.

iCan: I can explain why Abraham (pbuh) left Babylon and where he traveled.
I can say why someone travels with “to …” or “so that …”.
I can describe a journey in clear steps.

groupTask.title: From Babylon to the Valley

roles.name: Reader A (Babylon)
roles.job: You know Chapters 1 and 9: where the kingdom of Babylon was and who its king was.

roles.name: Reader B (Syria and Palestine)
roles.job: You know the first part of Chapter 10: why Abraham (pbuh) left Babylon and how he traveled.

roles.name: Reader C (The valley)
roles.job: You know the end of Chapter 10: who traveled to the lonely valley and which two hills were near it.

roles.name: Map Keeper
roles.job: You ask questions, draw the route on paper and write one reason next to each place.

steps: Each reader reads only his or her part and then closes the book.
The Map Keeper asks each reader three questions: Where was the place? Why did he go there? How did he travel?
Each reader answers with one sentence from the book, for example: “He traveled from Babylon to Syria and Palestine on camelback.” The Map Keeper adds the place and the reason to the route.
Together, check your route against the map page “Abraham’s Journey” in the app and correct anything you placed wrongly.
groupTask.share: Each group traces its route for the class (Babylon → Syria and Palestine → the valley of Safa and Marwa) and gives a reason for each move, using phrases such as “He decided to …” or “He traveled … to …”.
groupTask.solo: Cover Chapters 1–10, draw the route Babylon → Syria and Palestine → the valley of Safa and Marwa from memory with one reason for each move, then check it on the map page “Abraham’s Journey”.

pages.title: Hagar and Ishmael in the Valley
pages.content:
Abraham (pbuh) left them there and prayed to Allah to protect them. He said, “O our Lord! I have left my family to stay in a valley with no farming, near Your Holy House (the Ka’ba in Mecca); O Allah! Give them blessings so that they may give thanks.” (See Surah Ibrahim: 37.) Hagar knew that Abraham (pbuh) was doing what Allah told him.

She fearlessly said to Abraham (pbuh) when he left them in this desert valley, “Allah will never let us die; He will surely protect us.”

The valley had no trees, no fruit, no food, and no water. This was part of Allah’s plan to build the Holy House, the Ka’ba, and the city of Mecca in the time to come. But soon their food and water ran out. Hagar needed to feed her child. She helplessly started running from one hill to another looking for water and food. She ran between these two hills seven times. This effort by Hagar is known as “sa’y” in Hajj and Umrah rituals. Even today, Muslims must complete the ritual “sa’y” after performing the tawaf during Hajj or Umrah. This ritual involves walking back and forth between the hills of Safa and Marwa. Safa is about 130 meters from the Ka’ba, while Marwa is approximately 300 meters away.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-safa-and-marwa-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-kaaba-abraham
Bravely, without being afraid.
Was completely used up so none remained.
A religious action performed in a special way.
About a number or amount, but not exactly.

hotspots.title: Hagar’s Trust
hotspots.description: Hagar trusted that Allah would protect them in the desert valley.

hotspots.title: Safa and Marwa
hotspots.description: Hagar ran between the two hills seven times, and Muslims still perform this ritual, sa’y, in Hajj and Umrah.

exercises.title: Trust and Effort
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 11.
exercises.question: Hagar trusted Allah, so when the food and water ran out, she sat and waited for help.
exercises.explanation: Hagar trusted Allah: “Allah will never let us die; He will surely protect us.” But she did not only wait. She “started running from one hill to another looking for water and food” and “ran between these two hills seven times.”

feedback.correct: Correct! Hagar trusted Allah and also worked hard. She ran between Safa and Marwa seven times.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 11 again. What did Hagar do when the food and water ran out?

languageFocusExercises.title: Words for Hagar’s Struggle
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 11 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases tell us about Hagar’s situation and actions?

matchingPairs.left: their food and water ran out
matchingPairs.right: there was none left

matchingPairs.left: Hagar needed to feed her child
matchingPairs.right: it was necessary for her
began to move very fast
trying to find
without being afraid

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Run out” is a phrasal verb: when a supply runs out, it is all used up. “Need to + verb” shows necessity. “Start + -ing” and “begin to + verb” both mark the beginning of an action. “Look for” means “try to find”. The suffix -less means “without”, so “fearlessly” = without fear.

feedback.correct: Correct. You matched each phrase with its meaning in the chapter.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 11 again and replace each phrase with your answer. Does the sentence still make sense?

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose and Background
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from Chapter 11.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which forms show a purpose and an action that was going on at that time?

formChoices.sentence: Abraham (pbuh) left them there and prayed to Allah [choice] them.
Hagar knew that Abraham (pbuh) [choice] what Allah told him.
This was part of Allah’s plan [choice] the Holy House, the Ka’ba, and the city of Mecca in the time to come.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Pray to someone + to + verb” says what the prayer asks for: prayed to Allah to protect them. After a past verb such as “knew”, the past continuous shows an action that was going on at that time: Abraham was doing what Allah told him. “A plan + to + verb” names the purpose of the plan: Allah’s plan to build the Holy House. The prayer and Hagar’s own words in the chapter are read as they are and are not changed.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the forms for purpose and for an action in progress.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first and third paragraphs of Chapter 11 again. Which form names a purpose (to + verb)? Which form shows an action going on in the past?

languageFocusExercises.title: Explaining a Practice
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 11 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which phrases name a practice, give a rule, show order and say what it includes?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: This effort by Hagar [blank] “sa’y” in Hajj and Umrah rituals. Even today, Muslims [blank] complete the ritual “sa’y” [blank] performing the tawaf during Hajj or Umrah. This ritual [blank] walking back and forth between the hills of Safa and Marwa.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Explanations of a practice often use: The passive “is known as” to give its name; “must + base verb” (no “to”) for a rule; “after + -ing” to show which step comes first; and “involves + -ing” to say what the practice includes.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used the language of explaining a practice.
feedback.incorrect: Check the end of Chapter 11. The name is given with a passive form, and “must” is never followed by “to”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain a Process Clearly
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five sentences about a routine, a practice or a hard situation.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do people need to do, and in what order?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use so that, need to, start + -ing, look for, must, after + -ing, is known as, or involves + -ing when natural.

feedback.correct: Keep the five sentences connected as one short explanation rather than isolated examples.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give the situation or the aim.
discussionPrompts.example: Every year, our school organises a clean-up day in the local park.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give a need: “… need to …” or “… so that …”
discussionPrompts.example: We need to bring gloves and bags so that we can collect the rubbish safely.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Show a start: “… started …ing …”
discussionPrompts.example: At nine o’clock, everyone starts working in small groups.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Add a rule with “must”.
discussionPrompts.example: Every student must stay with the group and must not touch broken glass.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Say what happens next, or what it includes.
discussionPrompts.example: After collecting the rubbish, each group sorts it into plastic, paper and glass.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: How far is Safa from the Ka’ba?
beforeYouRead.quote: Safa is about 130 meters from the Ka’ba

iCan: I can tell how Hagar searched for water in the valley.
I can explain a practice with “is known as”, “must” and “after …”.
I can explain a routine or process step by step.

pages.title: Zamzam and the City of Mecca
pages.content:
But there was no water and nobody nearby to help her. While the little child Ishmael was crying with thirst and Hagar was running between the two hills, suddenly water started flowing from the ground under the feet of Ishmael. When Hagar saw this from a distance, she shouted, “Zamzam!” meaning “Flow slowly, stop!”

She was so happy. She drank the water, collected it, and fed her child. Later on, this water gained a lot of fame. This historic Zamzam spring still exists, and it has given water for thousands of years. The water is special because it was a gift from Allah in the middle of the desert. Ishmael and his mother began to live in the valley. More people came to settle there because of this sacred spring.

They started building up a city called Mecca. Meanwhile, Abraham (pbuh) visited Mecca several times to see his family.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:abraham-mecca-valley-ancient
__historical_entity__:abraham-zamzam
A strong need to drink water.
Moving steadily and continuously, like a river.
A place where water naturally comes from the ground.
To begin living permanently in a place.
Very special and important in religion.

hotspots.title: Zamzam Water
hotspots.description: Water suddenly flowed from the ground under the feet of Ishmael (pbuh), a gift from Allah in the desert.

hotspots.title: A Growing City
hotspots.description: More people came to settle near the sacred spring, and they started building Mecca.

exercises.title: From Water to a City
exercises.instructions: Put the events of Chapter 12 in the right order.
exercises.question: How did the valley change?

sequencingItems.text: Ishmael was crying with thirst while Hagar ran between the hills.
Water started flowing from the ground under Ishmael’s feet.
Hagar saw it from a distance and shouted, “Zamzam!”
Hagar drank the water, collected it and fed her child.
More people came to settle there and started building Mecca.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 12 moves from need to gift to a new city: Ishmael’s thirst, the water under his feet, Hagar’s shout, the first drink, and then people who came to settle “because of this sacred spring.”

feedback.correct: Great! One gift of water changed an empty valley into the city of Mecca.
feedback.incorrect: Start with Ishmael’s thirst. The city is built only after people come because of the water.

languageFocusExercises.title: Background and Sudden Event
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 12. Then choose the best explanation.
languageFocusExercises.question: “While the little child Ishmael was crying with thirst and Hagar was running between the two hills, suddenly water started flowing from the ground under the feet of Ishmael.” Why does the writer use “was crying” and “was running”, but “started flowing”?
options: “Was crying” and “was running” were already in progress; “started flowing” is the new event that happened during them.
“Was crying” and “was running” happened after the water started flowing from the ground under Ishmael’s feet.
“Was crying” and “was running” were very short actions that happened only once, one after the other.
“Started flowing” describes something that happened every day in the valley, before and after this.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “While + past continuous” (was crying, was running) sets the background: Actions already in progress. “Suddenly” + past simple (started flowing) introduces a new event that happens in the middle of them. The next sentence uses “When + past simple” for the moment that causes a reaction: “When Hagar saw this …, she shouted”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The continuous forms set the background, and the past simple brings in the sudden event.
feedback.incorrect: Look at “While” and “suddenly”. Which actions were happening already, and which one was new?

languageFocusExercises.title: Saw or Was Seeing?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap the wrong words, then choose the correction.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you correct verbs that should not be in the continuous form?

errorItems.sentence: When Hagar was seeing this from a distance, she shouted, “Zamzam!”
This historic Zamzam spring is still existing, and it has given water for thousands of years.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “When + past simple” marks a single moment that causes the next action: When Hagar saw this, she shouted. Verbs of perception and state, such as see and exist, are not normally used in the continuous. “Still + present simple” (still exists) shows that a situation continues from the past to now.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used simple forms for a single moment and for a continuing state.
feedback.incorrect: See and exist are usually not used with -ing. Check the first and second paragraphs of Chapter 12.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build a Cause Sentence
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Tap the pieces to build the sentence. You can start with the cause.
languageFocusExercises.question: What follows “because of”, and where can the cause go?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because of” is followed by a noun phrase (this sacred spring), not a clause. “Came to settle” uses to + verb for purpose: people came in order to live there. The cause can go at the end or at the start: “Because of this sacred spring, more people came to settle there.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You built the sentence with a clear cause and purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Start with who came (More people), then why they came (to settle there), then the cause (because of + noun). Check the second paragraph of Chapter 12.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain How a Place Changes
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five sentences about a place that changes over time.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was the place like, and how did it change?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use while, suddenly, when, still, because/because of, begin/start, come to + verb, and meanwhile where natural.

feedback.correct: Keep the sentences connected as one short development story.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Set the scene: “While …, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Thirty years ago, while most people in my grandfather’s village were working on farms, the main road was only a dusty path.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Add a new event with “suddenly” or “when”.
discussionPrompts.example: Then, one year, a big factory suddenly opened near the village.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Give a reason with “because” or “because of”.
discussionPrompts.example: Many young families moved there because of the new jobs.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Show what continues: “… still …”
discussionPrompts.example: The old stone bridge still stands over the river.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Show a later change with “began to”, “started to” or “meanwhile”.
discussionPrompts.example: Meanwhile, the village began to grow into a small town with a school and a hospital.

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What does “Zamzam” mean?
beforeYouRead.quote: When Hagar saw this from a distance, she shouted, “Zamzam!” meaning “Flow slowly, stop!”

I can show a background action and a sudden event with “while” and “suddenly”.
I can explain how a place changed over time.

pages.title: Building the Ka’ba
pages.content:
One day, Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to build the House of Allah, the Ka’ba. Abraham (pbuh) said to Ishmael, “O Ishmael, Allah told me to do an important task, and you will help me in this task.” Ishmael replied, “I will help you for sure.”

The Ka’ba was an ancient building originally built as the first sacred place on Earth (see Surah Al Imran: 96), but it disappeared over time. Father and son found the foundations of the old building and began to construct the new building on it.

After he built the Holy Ka’ba, Abraham’s (pbuh) mission was over. He built a place of worship for all people of different races and colors. Hajj reminds Muslims about many events of Allah’s beloved “friend,” Abraham (pbuh), and his family.

Over the centuries, Ishmael’s family grew bigger; among them was Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam (pbuh). They spread all over the Arabian Peninsula to carry their grandfather Abraham’s (pbuh) message of the Oneness of Allah. The message is “There is no god but Allah. He has no partner, He does not need any help, and nothing is like Him. Allah is unique in every way.”

__historical_entity__:abraham-kaaba-abraham
The strong base under a building.
To build something.
Groups of people with different backgrounds or physical traits.

hotspots.title: The Old Foundations
hotspots.description: Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael (pbuh) found the old foundations and built the Ka’ba on them.

hotspots.title: The Message of Oneness
hotspots.description: The family of Ishmael (pbuh) carried Abraham’s (pbuh) message of the Oneness of Allah, and Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) was one of them.

exercises.title: A House for Everyone
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 13, for whom did Abraham build the Ka’ba?
options: only for Abraham, Ishmael and their family
only for the people who settled near Zamzam
for all people of different races and colors
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says, “He built a place of worship for all people of different races and colors.” It connects this house with the message of the Oneness of Allah that Abraham’s family carried.

feedback.correct: Right! The chapter says the Ka’ba is a place of worship for people of every race and color.
feedback.incorrect: Read the third paragraph of Chapter 13 again. Find the words “a place of worship for …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Instruction or Promise?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Is each part an instruction, or a promise about the future? Sort the parts.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the opening dialogue move from an instruction to a promise?

dragDropGroups.group: What someone was told to do
items: Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to build the House of Allah
Allah told me to do an important task

dragDropGroups.group: What someone will do (a role or a promise)
items: you will help me in this task
I will help you for sure

What someone was told to do: Allah commanded Abraham (pbuh) to build the House of Allah
Allah told me to do an important task
What someone will do (a role or a promis: you will help me in this task
I will help you for sure

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Command/tell + person + to + verb reports an instruction (commanded Abraham to build, told me to do). “Will + verb” looks to the future: Abraham uses it to give Ishmael a role (you will help me), and Ishmael uses it to make a promise (I will help you for sure). “For sure” makes the promise stronger.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated reported instructions from future roles and promises.
feedback.incorrect: Look for command/told + person + to (an instruction) and will + verb (the future). Check the first paragraph of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: From Old Building to New
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the parts of Chapter 13 in order. Use the linking words to help you.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words show an earlier state, a change over time, a new start and completion?

sequencingItems.text: The Ka’ba was an ancient building originally built as the first sacred place on Earth,
but it disappeared over time.
Father and son found the foundations of the old building
and began to construct the new building on it.
After he built the Holy Ka’ba, Abraham’s (pbuh) mission was over.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: The past simple “was” describes the earlier state. “But … over time” shows a slow change. “The old building” refers back to the ancient Ka’ba, and “on it” refers to the foundations. “Began to” marks the start of the rebuilding, and “After + past simple” shows that one action was completed before the next.

feedback.correct: Correct. The linking words guided you from the old building to the completed mission.
feedback.incorrect: Look for clues: “but” and “and” continue a sentence, “the old building” and “on it” refer back, and “After he built …” comes when the work is finished.

languageFocusExercises.title: Purpose Across Generations
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines from Chapter 13 with words from the bank. Two words are not needed.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which words show who the Ka’ba was for, a long period of time and a purpose?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: He built a place of worship [blank] all people of different races and colors. … [blank], Ishmael’s family grew bigger; among them was Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam (pbuh). They spread all over the Arabian Peninsula [blank] carry their grandfather Abraham’s (pbuh) message of the Oneness of Allah.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “For + noun” shows who something is for (a place of worship for all people). “Over the centuries” shows change or continuity across a long period, here across generations. “To + verb” gives the purpose of an action (spread … to carry the message). “Since” needs a starting point, and “so” would introduce a result.

feedback.correct: Correct. You showed who the Ka’ba was for, the long time period and the purpose.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Who was the place for? How long did it take for children to have children? Why did they spread? Then check the last two paragraphs of Chapter 13.

languageFocusExercises.title: Explain How a Legacy Continues
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write or say five sentences about a project or tradition that lives on.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did the work start, and how does it continue?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: A strong response can use told/asked + person + to + verb, will, after, begin/start, to + verb for purpose, and over the years where natural.

feedback.correct: Keep the five sentences connected as one explanation of how something continues over time.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Say what someone was asked to do.
discussionPrompts.example: Ten years ago, our English teacher asked a group of students to start a reading club.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Say what someone will do: “… will …”
discussionPrompts.example: One student promised, “I will bring a new book every month.”

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say how the work started or was finished.
discussionPrompts.example: After they collected two hundred books, they opened a small library in an empty classroom.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Say what it is for: “… so that …” or “… for …”
discussionPrompts.example: The library is a quiet place for students to read and borrow books for free.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 5 — Show how it continues over the years.
discussionPrompts.example: Over the years, the teacher retired, but new students still run the club every week.

beforeYouRead.quote: Ishmael replied, “I will help you for sure.”

I can report an instruction and make a promise with “will”.
I can explain how a project or tradition continues over the years.

roles.name: Researcher
roles.job: You find out where your town or school gets its water and how the place grew around it.

legend.route:toSyriaPalestine: From Babylon to Syria and Palestine
legend.route:toValley: To the valley of Safa and Marwa

places.name: Babylon
places.text: About 4,000 years ago, a boy named Abraham lived in the kingdom of Babylon in Mesopotamia. It was his homeland. People there worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun and statues of wood and stone, and Nimrod was their king.
places.teacherNote: The book gives no exact year, only “about 4,000 years ago”. It does not name Abraham’s (pbuh) town; the pin marks the old city of Babylon. Mardukh, the chief god of Babylon, appears in chapter 2.
places.question: What did people in Babylon worship?

places.name: Mesopotamia
places.text: Mesopotamia was an old land between two rivers. The kingdom of Babylon was in Mesopotamia, so this was Abraham’s (pbuh) homeland.
places.teacherNote: The two rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates; the B1 story does not name them. The circle is only approximate, as there were no fixed borders.
places.question: Which kingdom was in Mesopotamia?

places.name: The great fire
places.text: Firewood was collected for days, and the fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it. News about it traveled very fast and far, so people came from many different towns. Abraham (pbuh) was thrown into the flames, but Allah made the fire cool and safe for him.
places.teacherNote: The book does not say where the fire was, so the pin beside Babylon only shows the event. After the miracle, Abraham (pbuh) met Nimrod, the king of Babylon (chapter 9).
places.question: Why did Abraham (pbuh) stay calm before the fire?

places.name: Syria
places.text: Nobody in Babylon was going to listen to Abraham’s (pbuh) message, so he decided to travel to other lands. He traveled from Babylon to Syria and Palestine on camelback. It was a long, hot and tiring journey.
places.teacherNote: In Abraham’s (pbuh) time this was a wide region, not the country of today. The circle is approximate. The Arabic edition says سوريا.
places.question: Why did Abraham (pbuh) leave Babylon?

places.name: Palestine
places.text: Palestine and Syria were the lands on Abraham’s (pbuh) journey from Babylon. He traveled to these lands to spread Allah’s message. Later, Allah commanded him to travel with his wife Hagar and their little son Ishmael.
places.teacherNote: The book says Abraham (pbuh) married Hagar and Ishmael was born “during his journey”, but not where. It also does not say where the family started the journey to the valley; the line is drawn from the Palestine area.
places.question: Why did Abraham (pbuh) travel to other lands?

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Abraham (pbuh) left Hagar and Ishmael in a lonely desert valley near two small hills, Safa and Marwa. Hagar ran between the hills seven times, and then Zamzam water started flowing from the ground. People came to settle near the spring and built the city of Mecca. Later, Abraham (pbuh) and Ishmael built the Ka’ba here.
places.teacherNote: Safa is about 130 meters from the Ka’ba and Marwa about 300 meters (chapter 11). Hagar’s running is remembered as sa’y in Hajj and Umrah. Abraham (pbuh) visited Mecca several times; the book does not say where he came from.
places.question: Why did people come to settle in this valley?

places.name: Arabian Peninsula
places.text: Over the centuries, Ishmael’s family grew bigger, and Muhammad, the Prophet of Islam (pbuh), was among them. They spread all over the Arabian Peninsula and carried Abraham’s (pbuh) message of the Oneness of Allah.
places.teacherNote: The circle is only approximate. The Arabic edition says “the years passed” where the English says “over the centuries”.
places.question: What message did Ishmael’s family carry?

challenge.prompt: Find Babylon, Abraham’s (pbuh) homeland in Mesopotamia.
Find Syria. Abraham (pbuh) traveled there from Babylon on camelback.
Find Palestine. Abraham (pbuh) traveled there from Babylon, as he did to Syria.
Find Mecca. A spring of water appeared there in the middle of the desert.
Find the Arabian Peninsula. Ishmael’s family spread all over it.

pages.title: Knowledge Check
pages.content: Check your whole-story understanding with eight evidence-based questions.

exercises.title: A Young Man’s Search
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 3, as a young man Abraham still thought that Allah might be a statue.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Although he always wondered about Allah, he also knew that Allah could not be a statue.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. He was still searching for the Creator, but he already knew that Allah could not be a statue.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the first paragraph of Chapter 3. What did Abraham already know while he was searching?

exercises.title: A New Duty
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 4.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham begin to guide his people after that morning?
options: His father asked him to explain the idols.
The people of Babylon asked him for help.
Allah had chosen him to be His Messenger.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “He recognized that he should guide his people because Allah chose him to be His Messenger.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Once Allah chose him as His Messenger, guiding his people became his duty, starting with his own father.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the short paragraph after Abraham’s prayer in Chapter 4. What did he recognize, and why?

exercises.title: A Joke with a Message
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 6.
exercises.question: Abraham jokingly asked the statues, “Why don’t you eat the food?” What was the point of his joke?
options: Giving food to statues that cannot eat was foolish.
The people had forgotten to bring enough food.
He wanted the statues to share the food with him.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “Abraham (pbuh) jokingly asked them, “Why don’t you eat the food? It is getting cold.” Offering food to these statues was so ridiculous.”

feedback.correct: Well done. The joke shows the problem in one question: The statues could not eat, so offering them food made no sense.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the end of the first paragraph of Chapter 6. Read the sentence that comes right after Abraham’s question.

exercises.title: “Nothing from You!”
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 8.
exercises.question: Angel Gabriel asked Abraham in the fire, “Is there anything you wish for?” What does Abraham’s answer show?
options: He did not believe that Gabriel was an angel.
He trusted Allah alone, not even an angel.
He wanted to show the people he was brave.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “Angel Gabriel came to him and asked, “Is there anything you wish for?” Abraham (pbuh) only said, “Nothing from you!”” Earlier in the chapter: “He knew that Allah would never leave him alone.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham asked for nothing from anyone but Allah. The chapter says he knew Allah would never leave him alone.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 8 about why Abraham stayed calm. Then connect it with his words to Gabriel.

exercises.title: Nimrod Meets Abraham
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: Nimrod called Abraham to him because he wanted to believe in Allah.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 9: “He realized that Abraham was not an ordinary person, so he decided to meet him.” Later he claims, “I can give life and death,” and the debate “made Nimrod even more angry.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is false. Nimrod saw that Abraham was not ordinary, but he met him to challenge him, not to believe.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the Nimrod paragraphs in Chapter 9. Why did Nimrod decide to meet Abraham, and how did he feel at the end?

exercises.title: An Empty Valley
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 11.
exercises.question: The valley had no trees, no food and no water. How does Chapter 11 explain this?
options: Abraham wanted to test how strong Hagar was.
It was part of Allah’s plan for the Ka’ba and Mecca.
The people of Babylon had cut down all the trees.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “The valley had no trees, no fruit, no food, and no water. This was part of Allah’s plan to build the Holy House, the Ka’ba, and the city of Mecca in the time to come.”

feedback.correct: Correct. The empty valley was not an accident: It was where the Ka’ba and Mecca would later be built.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the start of the third paragraph of Chapter 11. What does the sentence after “no water” say?

exercises.title: Zamzam Today
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false according to the story.
exercises.question: According to Chapter 12, the Zamzam spring still gives water today.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 12: “This historic Zamzam spring still exists, and it has given water for thousands of years.”

feedback.correct: Right, the statement is true. The spring that appeared under Ishmael’s feet has given water for thousands of years.
feedback.incorrect: Reread the second paragraph of Chapter 12. What does it say about the Zamzam spring today?

exercises.title: The Message Continues
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer. Use the evidence in Chapter 13.
exercises.question: What did Ishmael’s family do, according to the last paragraph of the story?
options: They carried Abraham’s message of the Oneness of Allah.
They went back to Babylon to find Abraham’s people.
They built new idols around the Ka’ba in Mecca.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13: “They spread all over the Arabian Peninsula to carry their grandfather Abraham’s (pbuh) message of the Oneness of Allah.”

feedback.correct: Correct. Abraham’s message did not end with him: His family, and later Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), carried it on.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Reread the last paragraph of Chapter 13. Where did Ishmael’s family go, and what did they carry?

vocabulary.definition: The country or place where a person comes from.
vocabulary.storyExample: In his homeland, people worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun, and statues made from wood and stone.

vocabulary.definition: Able to learn, understand, and think well.
vocabulary.storyExample: He could not understand how an intelligent person could make a statue and then see it as a god which could help or harm him.

vocabulary.definition: Asking strongly for help or something needed.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham was surprised to see that when people entered the building, they bowed to the statues and started crying and begging.

vocabulary.definition: Bent the head or body forward to show respect or worship.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham was surprised to see that when people entered the building, they bowed to the statues and started crying and begging.

vocabulary.definition: To pray to someone or something and show it great love and respect.
vocabulary.storyExample: In his homeland, people worshipped the stars, the moon, the sun, and statues made from wood and stone.

vocabulary.definition: A person whose job is to carve statues that people worship.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham’s father was an idol maker, named Azer.

vocabulary.definition: Helpful acts or good things given to someone.
vocabulary.storyExample: We ask favors from them and give them presents.

vocabulary.definition: A feeling that someone or something is important and deserves honor.
vocabulary.storyExample: We worship them; we show love and respect to them.

vocabulary.definition: Hit something with the foot.
vocabulary.storyExample: But Abraham used to play with these idols as toys; he rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them.

vocabulary.definition: The One who brought everything into existence and controls it.
vocabulary.storyExample: On the other hand, Abraham was in search of one true Creator.

vocabulary.definition: Land outside towns and cities.
vocabulary.storyExample: One night, Abraham left his home to take a walk in the countryside.

vocabulary.definition: A natural hollow place in a mountain or rock.
vocabulary.storyExample: On a nearby mountain, he found a cave, sat there, and started thinking about Allah.

vocabulary.definition: Gradually became less visible or disappeared.
vocabulary.storyExample: But when the moon faded, he understood that it could not be his Lord.

vocabulary.definition: The time when the sun first appears in the morning.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham stayed until sunrise, and when he saw the bright sun, he wondered, “Could this be my Lord? It is bigger.”

vocabulary.definition: Everything Allah has made, such as the sun, the moon and the stars.
vocabulary.storyExample: But when it set, he understood that Allah could not be one of the creations.

vocabulary.definition: Put the forehead to the ground in worship.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham prostrated himself and asked Allah for help.

vocabulary.definition: To throw rocks at someone to hurt or kill them.
vocabulary.storyExample: If you do not stop speaking like this, I will stone you.

vocabulary.definition: To stop trying to do something.
vocabulary.storyExample: Abraham (pbuh) did not give up and told them, “My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them, and heals me when I am sick.

vocabulary.definition: To hurt or damage someone or something.
vocabulary.storyExample: They have no power to help or harm you.

vocabulary.definition: Makes a sick or injured person well again.
vocabulary.storyExample: My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them, and heals me when I am sick.

vocabulary.definition: To think again about an idea or belief.
vocabulary.storyExample: He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs.

vocabulary.definition: Lack of good sense or wise thinking.
vocabulary.storyExample: Prophet Abraham (pbuh) decided to show them the foolishness of their beliefs.

vocabulary.definition: A special event when people gather for a happy occasion.
vocabulary.storyExample: There was a big celebration soon.

vocabulary.definition: A tool with a sharp metal head used for cutting.
vocabulary.storyExample: All the people usually went outside of town, so he got an axe and waited until the whole town was empty.

vocabulary.definition: Very silly or unreasonable.
vocabulary.storyExample: Offering food to these statues was so ridiculous.

vocabulary.definition: Broken violently into many pieces.
vocabulary.storyExample: They all gathered around the smashed idols.

vocabulary.definition: Unhappy or annoyed about something.
vocabulary.storyExample: The people were displeased with what they heard and said, “You are well aware that these idols don’t speak!”

vocabulary.definition: A painful feeling caused by knowing something is wrong.
vocabulary.storyExample: They looked at each other in shame because their thoughts and feelings told them that Abraham (pbuh) was right.

vocabulary.definition: Too proud to accept the truth or a mistake.
vocabulary.storyExample: But they were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth and admit they were wrong.

vocabulary.definition: Wood that is cut and used to make a fire.
vocabulary.storyExample: Firewood was collected for the fire for days.

vocabulary.definition: To come near something or someone.
vocabulary.storyExample: The fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it.

vocabulary.definition: The bright, burning parts of a fire.
vocabulary.storyExample: The heat was so strong that even birds couldn’t fly over the rising flames.

vocabulary.definition: An old machine used to throw heavy objects.

vocabulary.definition: People whose job is to protect a person or place.

vocabulary.definition: Normal and not unusual or special.

vocabulary.definition: Strong belief and trust in Allah.

vocabulary.definition: To make an idea or message reach more people.
