vocabulary.definition: Bravely, without being afraid.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the grammar patterns, discourse relationships, and communicative functions developed across all thirteen chapters.

exercises.title: Notice: Habit, Background or Event?
exercises.instructions: A habit, a background action, or one event? Put each part in the right group.
exercises.question: Which parts are habits, background actions or single events?

items: But Abraham used to play with these idols as toys …
All the people usually went outside of town …
… they were still showing love and respect to idols.
While the little child Ishmael was crying with thirst …

dragDropGroups.group: One event that moves the story on
items: One day, his father saw Abraham riding the statue of Mardukh …
… suddenly water started flowing from the ground …
Finally, they reached a lonely valley …

A habit in the past: But Abraham used to play with these idols as toys …
All the people usually went outside of town …
An action in progress (background): … they were still showing love and respect to idols.
While the little child Ishmael was crying with thirst …
One event that moves the story on: One day, his father saw Abraham riding the statue of Mardukh …
… suddenly water started flowing from the ground …
Finally, they reached a lonely valley …

exercises.explanation: Used to + verb and usually + past simple describe what happened again and again in an earlier time (Chapters 2 and 6). Was/were + -ing describes an action in progress, the background of the scene: The people were still showing respect to idols (Chapter 3), Ishmael was crying (Chapter 12). The past simple, often with One day, suddenly or Finally, tells the single event that moves the story on. Careful: In “his father saw Abraham riding the statue”, the event is saw; riding only describes what Abraham was doing at that moment.

feedback.correct: Well done. You separated habits, background actions and single events across the whole book.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb form in each part: used to / usually, was/were + -ing, or a past simple event with a time word such as One day, suddenly or Finally.

exercises.title: Notice: What Does “Could” Do?
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from the book. Match each one with what “could” means.
exercises.question: The book uses “could” again and again. Does it always mean the same thing?

matchingPairs.left: … see it as a god which could help or harm him.
matchingPairs.right: an ability that people wrongly believed in

matchingPairs.left: He saw a bright star and wondered, “Could this be my Lord?”
matchingPairs.right: an idea that is being tested with a question

matchingPairs.left: The fire was so big that people couldn’t approach it.
matchingPairs.right: a real limit: Nobody was able to do it

matchingPairs.left: … so that his child could teach people about Allah.
matchingPairs.right: the aim of a request: an ability in the future

correctAnswer.… see it as a god which could help or ha: an ability that people wrongly believed in
correctAnswer.He saw a bright star and wondered, “Coul: an idea that is being tested with a question
correctAnswer.The fire was so big that people couldn’t: a real limit: Nobody was able to do it
correctAnswer.… so that his child could teach people a: the aim of a request: an ability in the future

exercises.explanation: Could changes its job with the context. In Chapter 1 it describes a power people believed a statue had, while the chapter shows the truth: “They could not even move from one place to another on their own.” In Chapter 3, Could this be …? tests a possible answer, and Abraham rejects it when the star sets. In Chapter 8, couldn’t is a real limit: The heat stopped people. In Chapter 10, so that + could gives the aim of Abraham’s request: what his child would be able to do later.

feedback.correct: Correct. The same small word can show a belief, a test, a real limit or an aim.
feedback.incorrect: Read each sentence again and ask: Is someone believing, testing an idea, meeting a real limit, or hoping for something in the future?

exercises.title: Notice: Looking Forward from the Past
exercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapters 6, 8 and 10. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 6: “He made a plan to destroy all their idols, but he did not tell anyone what he was going to do.” Chapter 8: “He knew that Allah would never leave him alone …” Chapter 10: “Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message.” What do “was going to” and “would” show in these sentences?
options: an action that was already finished at that moment
a habit that was repeated again and again in the past
the future, seen from a moment in the past
an action that was in progress at that exact moment
exercises.explanation: The book is told in the past, so when it looks forward from a past moment it uses was/were going to + verb and would + verb. When Abraham made his plan, breaking the idols was still in the future. Before the fire, Abraham trusted what would happen next. In Chapter 10, he understood a prediction about the future. In his own words at that moment, these would be is going to and will.

feedback.correct: Correct. Was going to and would are the future seen from the past.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: At the moment described, had the action happened yet? Was it still in the future?

exercises.title: Build: Reason, Result and Surprise
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines from the book with words from the bank. Two are not needed.
exercises.question: Which word gives a reason, which gives a result, and which show an unexpected contrast?
exercises.fillBlanksText: He recognized that he should guide his people [blank] Allah chose him to be His Messenger. … People felt embarrassed by the miracle, [blank] their anger and arrogance remained unchanged. Prophet Abraham (pbuh) tried every way to show them their error; [blank], their rage didn’t calm down. … Abraham (pbuh) realized that nobody was going to listen to his message. [blank], he decided to leave Babylon …
exercises.explanation: Because + a clause gives the reason for a duty or a decision; because of needs a noun, not a clause. Yet (between two clauses, no comma after it) and however (after a semicolon, with a comma after it) both show a contrast we do not expect: People were embarrassed, but they did not change. Therefore starts a new sentence and gives the result of what came before: Nobody would listen, so Abraham left. In the first gap, so would turn the reason into a result.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked reasons, results and unexpected contrasts, and you placed them correctly in the sentence.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next part give a reason, a result, or a surprising contrast? Then check the punctuation around the gap. Look again at Chapters 4, 9 and 10.

exercises.title: Build: What Follows the Verb?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: After “was surprised”, “made him” and “told his wife”, which form comes next?

formChoices.sentence: Abraham was surprised [choice] that when people entered the building, they bowed to the statues …
It made him [choice] to see the people of the kingdom …
Prophet Abraham (pbuh) told his wife [choice] near one of the hills with Ishmael.

exercises.explanation: An adjective of feeling + to + verb gives the cause of the feeling: surprised to see (Chapter 1). Make + person + adjective shows how something changes a person’s feelings: It made him sad (Chapter 3). Tell + person + to + verb reports an instruction (Chapter 10), like “He ordered his guards to bring two slaves” in Chapter 9. Compare make and let, which take the base verb with no to: “Can you make the sun rise from the west?”

feedback.correct: Correct. Surprised to + verb, made + person + adjective, told + person + to + verb.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the word just before the gap: a feeling adjective, make + person, or tell + person. Check Chapters 1, 3 and 10.

exercises.title: Build: Fix the Verb Form
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake in a verb. Tap it, then choose the correction.
exercises.question: Can you fix the verb forms?

errorItems.sentence: But the statues could not heard or understand these prayers and wishes!
Prophet Abraham’s (pbuh) hands and feet was tied, and he was placed on a catapult.
… he got an axe and waited until the whole town will be empty.

exercises.explanation: After a modal we use the base verb: could not + hear (Chapter 1). The passive is be + past participle, and the form of be agrees with the subject: hands and feet (plural) were tied (Chapter 8); the passive is used because the people who did it are not important here. After until, when, after and while, we do not use will or would for the future: The past simple does this job in a story, so he waited until the town was empty (Chapter 6).

feedback.correct: Well done. You corrected the verb after could not, the passive form and the verb after until.
feedback.incorrect: Check what comes after could not, whether the subject is singular or plural, and which tense follows until in a past story. Compare with Chapters 1, 6 and 8.

exercises.title: Build: Report What People Said
exercises.instructions: Report each sentence from Chapters 2, 5 and 7. Write the missing words.
exercises.question: What changes when we report a statement or a question?

transformItems.source: Azer replied, “They are not toys, but our gods.”
transformItems.frame: Azer replied that they [blank] toys, but their gods.

transformItems.source: People replied, “We saw our fathers worship them; …”
transformItems.frame: People replied that they [blank] their fathers worship them.

transformItems.source: They asked him, “Did you harm our gods in this way?”
transformItems.frame: They asked him [blank] their gods in that way.

exercises.explanation: In reported speech the pronouns change (our → their, you → he), and the verb usually moves one step back: are → were, saw → had seen, did you harm → had harmed. A yes/no question is reported with if or whether and statement word order, with no did and no question mark. Inside a longer sentence, a question idea also uses statement word order, as in Chapter 7: the people “tried to find out who did this”.

feedback.correct: Correct. You changed the pronouns, moved the verbs back and reported the question with if or whether.
feedback.incorrect: Change our to their and you to he. Move the verb back one step, and use if or whether for a yes/no question.

exercises.title: Use: Our Recycling Project
exercises.instructions: This text is new. Complete it with words from the bank. Three are not needed.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s language to tell the story of a class project?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Last year, many students in our class [blank] throw paper into the rubbish bin. One day, our teacher, Mrs Demir, asked us to make a recycling box. We made a plan, but we did not tell the other classes what we [blank] to do. At first, some students laughed at the idea. We did not give up, [blank]. After two months, the box was [blank] full that we needed a second one. Now, every Friday, the paper [blank] to a recycling center in our town.
exercises.explanation: Used to + verb describes a past habit that has now stopped (use to is only correct after did/didn’t). Were going to is the future seen from the past: The plan was still in the future. Though at the end of a sentence shows a contrast. So + adjective + that gives a strong degree and its result (such needs a noun: such a full box). The paper is taken is passive: What happens to the paper matters, not who takes it.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language to tell a new story.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap ask: A past habit? the future seen from the past? a contrast? a degree and its result? something that happens to the paper?

exercises.title: Use: Check a Friend’s Sentences
exercises.instructions: A friend wrote these sentences. Each has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correction.
exercises.question: Can you use the rules from the book to correct new sentences?

errorItems.sentence: Our coach made us to run around the school field three times.
The maths exam was such difficult that nobody finished it early.
My teacher asked me if did I finish my project.

exercises.explanation: Make + person + base verb, with no to: made us run. So + adjective + that shows a degree and its result; such needs a noun (such a difficult exam). A reported question uses if + statement word order and moves the verb back: asked me if I had finished.

feedback.correct: Well done. You can check your own writing with the book’s patterns.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: Which verbs take the base form? Is there a noun after such? Is the reported question in statement word order?

exercises.title: Use: A Plan That Changed Something
exercises.instructions: Write five or six sentences about a plan that changed your life. Tell a partner first.
exercises.question: What was the plan, and what did it change?
exercises.explanation: Example: Two years ago, the children in our street used to play on a dirty piece of land. One day, while we were cleaning our bikes, our neighbor Mr Aydın told us to write to the town council. We sent a letter, but we did not know what they were going to say. However, they said yes, so the rubbish was collected and new trees were planted. The park was so beautiful that everybody came to see it. Today we still play there every afternoon.

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: used to for a past habit, while + was/were -ing for the background, told/asked + person + to, was/were going to, a passive (was/were + past participle), a linker (however, so, because) and so … that.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 1–2 — Before: “We used to …” “One day, while we were …ing, …”
discussionPrompts.example: Our school garden used to be full of rubbish and broken bottles. One day, while we were playing football next to it, our class decided to clean it.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — The plan: “… asked us to …” “We didn’t know what we were going to …”
discussionPrompts.example: Our teacher asked us to make a plan, but we didn’t know what we were going to plant.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — The work: “… was cleaned / painted / planted”, with “however”, “so” or “because”
discussionPrompts.example: The rubbish was collected and the walls were painted, but the soil was very dry, so we watered it every day.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentences 5–6 — The result: “It was so … that …” “Today … still …”
discussionPrompts.example: In spring, the garden was so beautiful that other classes came to visit it. Today, we still look after it every Friday.

pages.title: Final Challenge
pages.content: Demonstrate B1-level understanding across the complete story.

exercises.title: Guided Before Guiding
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Before Abraham began to guide his people, he himself asked Allah to show him the right way.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 says: “Abraham prostrated himself and asked Allah for help.” He said: “If Allah doesn’t show me the right way, I will be on the wrong path.” Only then: “He recognized that he should guide his people because Allah chose him to be His Messenger.”

feedback.correct: True. Abraham first asked for guidance, and then he guided others.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second and third paragraphs of Chapter 4. What did Abraham do before he went to his father?

exercises.title: Food, Drink and Healing
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason the story supports.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham tell the people that his Lord gives him food and drink and heals him?
options: to ask the people for food and medicine
to show that their statues had no such power
to explain why he was not hungry at the festival
exercises.explanation: In Chapter 5 Abraham says: “My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them, and heals me when I am sick. Your statues have no power to do these.”

feedback.correct: Yes. He compared Allah’s care with the statues’ weakness, so the people could see the difference.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence right after Abraham’s words about food and healing. What does he say about the statues?

exercises.title: Think Again
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 5 with one word: reconsider, forget or hide.
exercises.question: What did Abraham want the people to do?
exercises.fillBlanksText: He wanted them to [blank] their beliefs.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 says: “He wanted them to reconsider their beliefs. They ignored him, though.” Abraham gave them reasons so they would think again.

feedback.correct: Yes. “Reconsider” means to think about something again, maybe to change it.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of Chapter 5. What did Abraham hope the people would do with their beliefs?

exercises.title: A Secret Plan
exercises.instructions: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
exercises.question: Abraham kept his plan secret before the big celebration.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6 says: “He made a plan to destroy all their idols, but he did not tell anyone what he was going to do.”

feedback.correct: Right. He did not tell anyone and waited until the town was empty.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentences of Chapter 6. Did Abraham tell anyone about his plan?

exercises.title: Abraham’s Path
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: How does Abraham’s story develop from his childhood to his last mission?

sequencingItems.text: Abraham is thrown into the fire, but it becomes safe for him.
Young Abraham laughs at Azer’s words about Mardukh’s big ears.
Abraham and Ishmael build the Ka’ba on the old foundations.
Abraham breaks the idols while the town is empty.
Abraham asks Nimrod to make the sun rise from the west.
Abraham watches the star, the moon and the sun disappear.

exercises.explanation: Mardukh (Chapter 2), the sky (Chapters 3–4), the broken idols (Chapter 6), the fire (Chapter 8), Nimrod (Chapter 9) and the Ka’ba (Chapter 13). Nimrod “also heard about the miracle” before he called Abraham.

feedback.correct: Yes. Each step shows Abraham facing a bigger challenge, from his father’s house to the king.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Nimrod called Abraham after he “heard about the miracle” of the fire.

exercises.title: Evidence and What It Shows
exercises.instructions: Match each piece of evidence with what it shows.
exercises.question: What does each piece of evidence prove in the story?

matchingPairs.left: The star, the moon and the sun all set.
matchingPairs.right: They are creations, not the Creator.

matchingPairs.left: The statues cannot speak, see or protect themselves.
matchingPairs.right: They do not deserve to be worshipped.

matchingPairs.left: Nimrod cannot make the sun rise from the west.
matchingPairs.right: Only Allah has power over the sun.

matchingPairs.left: Abraham comes out of the fire unharmed.
matchingPairs.right: Allah does not leave alone the one who trusts Him.

They are creations, not the Creator.
correctAnswer.The statues cannot speak, see or protect: They do not deserve to be worshipped.
correctAnswer.Nimrod cannot make the sun rise from the: Only Allah has power over the sun.
Allah does not leave alone the one who trusts Him.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “he understood that Allah could not be one of the creations.” Chapter 7: “Then why do you worship things that can’t speak or see or even protect themselves?” Chapter 9: “Nimrod was unable to do this; only Allah has the power to do that.” Chapter 8: “He knew that Allah would never leave him alone”, and he “emerged in good condition”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Abraham’s arguments and the miracle all point to the same truth: Only Allah deserves worship.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the end of each scene in Chapters 4, 7, 8 and 9. What did it show?

exercises.title: Shame Without Change
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that connects the two chapters.
exercises.question: What do Chapters 7 and 9 both show about the people of Babylon?
options: They felt shame, but their arrogance did not change.
After the miracle, they finally accepted Abraham.
They were never ashamed of what they did.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “They looked at each other in shame … But they were so arrogant that they couldn’t accept the truth”. Chapter 9: “People felt embarrassed by the miracle, yet their anger and arrogance remained unchanged.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Two times they felt that Abraham was right, and two times their pride stopped them.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the last paragraph of Chapter 7 with the first paragraph of Chapter 9. What stayed the same?

exercises.title: A Child for the Mission
exercises.instructions: Choose the reason the story gives.
exercises.question: Why did Abraham ask Allah for a child?
options: so that he would not travel alone to Syria
so that the child could help Hagar find water
so that the child could teach people about Allah
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says Abraham “asked for a child from Allah so that his child could teach people about Allah.” At the end of the book, Ishmael’s family “carry their grandfather Abraham’s (pbuh) message”.

feedback.correct: Yes. Abraham’s wish for a child was part of his mission, not only a family wish.
feedback.incorrect: Read the sentence about Hagar and the child in Chapter 10. Find the words “so that”.

exercises.title: Signs in Mecca
exercises.instructions: Match each name with what the story tells about it.
exercises.question: What does the story tell about each of these?

matchingPairs.right: Hagar’s run between Safa and Marwa, seven times
the water that flowed under Ishmael’s feet
a city built by people who settled near the spring
a new building on the foundations of an ancient one

correctAnswer.sa’y: Hagar’s run between Safa and Marwa, seven times
correctAnswer.Zamzam: the water that flowed under Ishmael’s feet
correctAnswer.Mecca: a city built by people who settled near the spring
correctAnswer.the Ka’ba: a new building on the foundations of an ancient one

exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “She ran between these two hills seven times.” This effort “is known as “sa’y” in Hajj and Umrah rituals.” Chapter 12: “water started flowing from the ground under the feet of Ishmael”; “More people came to settle there because of this sacred spring. They started building up a city called Mecca.” Chapter 13: “Father and son found the foundations of the old building and began to construct the new building on it.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Places and rituals in Mecca today still carry the memory of Abraham’s family.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the second half of Chapter 11, Chapter 12 and the second paragraph of Chapter 13.

exercises.title: Allah’s Friend
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 13 with one word: friend, father or king.
exercises.question: How does Chapter 13 describe Abraham?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Hajj reminds Muslims about many events of Allah’s beloved “[blank],” Abraham (pbuh), and his family.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “Hajj reminds Muslims about many events of Allah’s beloved “friend,” Abraham (pbuh), and his family.”

feedback.correct: Yes. The story calls Abraham Allah’s beloved friend.
feedback.incorrect: Read the end of the third paragraph of Chapter 13. How is Abraham described?
